seed.conflict: after a surprising success that makes things harder
seed.openingStyle: 구체적인 사물이나 동작으로 시작(관사 The 로 시작하지 말 것)
seed.topicSeed: a train compartment in Auckland; a retired sailor and his neighbor after a surprising success that makes things harder

g.passage: Folding his newspaper into a hard square, Hemi informed the compartment that Tane had never in his life tied a decent knot. Tane, opposite, went on polishing the brass medal the regatta committee had pinned to him that morning, and Hemi added that the wind had done the sailing and Tane had merely sat in the boat taking credit for the weather. A clerk two seats down laughed. Hemi did not laugh. He had not meant it as a joke, exactly; it was more the sort of thing a man says to keep his hands busy. When the train lurched past Newmarket, the medal slid from Tane's knee. Hemi caught it before it reached the floor, wiped the ribbon on his own sleeve, and kept it in his fist until the platform. Tane's name would be in tomorrow's paper, and the wharf would talk of little else. On the platform Hemi tucked the medal into his neighbor's breast pocket, buttoned the flap shut, and walked ahead to find them a cab.
g.question: Which choice best describes Hemi's attitude toward Tane as conveyed in the text?
options: Dismissive of Tane's victory while eager to keep the joke going
Attentive to Tane while mainly worried about the attention ahead
Quietly proud of Tane while hiding it behind gruff complaints
Doubtful that Tane earned the medal while careful to protect it
g.explanation: 앞부분에서 Hemi는 Tane의 매듭 실력과 우승을 깎아내리지만, 곧 그것이 농담도 진심도 아닌 '손을 바쁘게 하려는 말'이라고 스스로 정정한다. 뒷부분에서 그는 떨어진 메달을 받아 소매로 닦고 끝까지 쥐고 있다가 Tane의 주머니에 넣어 단추까지 채워 준다. 말투와 행동의 어긋남을 합치면 투박한 불평 아래 숨은 자부심이 드러나므로 C가 정답이다. A는 말투만 읽은 해석이고, B는 신문·부두 이야기를 근거로 이유를 걱정으로 바꾼 것이며, D는 정정 어구와 맞지 않게 불평을 진심으로 받아들인 것이다.

seed.relationship: a priest and a lapsed parishioner
seed.conflict: over a recipe that was never written down
seed.topicSeed: a flooded cellar in Cairo; a priest and a lapsed parishioner over a recipe that was never written down

g.passage: Father Mohan cannot cook. He has told me so himself, three times, while standing in my cellar up to his shins in Nile water and asking about my mother's lentil bread. I said the recipe went into the ground with her, which was not a lie, exactly, since she never measured anything and I only ever watched. He nodded and lifted another sack of flour onto the shelf above the waterline. For a man who preaches at me every feast day, he carries flour poorly; half of it was paste by noon. When he had gone, I found the sacks stacked by weight, the ruined ones set apart, and a pencil note on the lid of the bread tin asking only what she had used in place of salt. I kept the note. On Sunday, I set a loaf on the vestry step before the bells, and went home by the long road so as not to pass his door.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Father Mohan?
options: Mildly mocking of Mohan's efforts while weary of his preaching
Warm toward Mohan while driven mainly by guilt about her mother
Skeptical of Mohan's cooking while curious about his pencil note
Grudgingly appreciative of Mohan's help while unwilling to say so
g.explanation: 화자는 앞부분에서 Mohan이 요리를 못하고 밀가루도 서툴게 나른다며 건조하게 비꼰다. 중간의 '거짓말은 아니었다, 정확히는'이라는 정정은 화자가 레시피를 완전히 닫아 버린 것은 아님을 암시한다. 뒷부분에서 화자는 그의 쪽지를 간직하고 빵을 몰래 두고 오되 그의 집 앞은 피해 돌아간다. 따라서 마지못한 고마움을 드러내지 않으려는 태도인 D가 정답이며, A는 말투만, B는 이유를 어머니에 대한 죄책감으로 바꾼 것, C는 지문 어휘(cooking, note)를 빌린 일반화다.

seed.conflict: over a borrowed object never returned

g.passage: Flour dust on the counter showed every mark of Astrid's borrowed fountain pen, which she had been tapping since six. I had lent it to her at the notary's office in March, for one signature, and I reminded her of this whenever we met, usually while she was mispronouncing 'gracias' to someone who spoke perfect English. Clients like Astrid keep interpreters humble; they also keep us broke. I wanted the pen back, or I told myself I did, which is not quite the same. When the baker came out with the first trays, Astrid asked me how to say that the bread smelled like her grandmother's kitchen. I gave her the words slowly, twice, and let her say them herself. Later, when she reached for the pen to sign for the order, I looked at the window and asked the baker about the weather in the hills.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Astrid?
options: Affectionate toward Astrid while posing as a put-upon creditor
Irritated by Astrid's habits while resigned to losing the pen
Patient with Astrid while hoping to earn her future business
Humble about her own work while still wanting the pen back
g.explanation: 화자는 앞부분에서 펜을 빌려 간 일을 매번 상기시키고 Astrid의 서툰 스페인어와 수입 문제를 투덜거린다. 중간에 '돌려받고 싶다고 스스로에게 말했을 뿐'이라는 정정이 나와 불평이 진심이 아님을 내비친다. 뒷부분에서 화자는 Astrid가 직접 말하도록 단어를 천천히 가르쳐 주고, 그녀가 펜을 쓰려 할 때 일부러 시선을 돌려 화제를 피한다. 그러므로 빚쟁이 행세 아래 애정이 깔린 A가 정답이며, B는 말투만, C는 이유를 금전적 이익으로 바꾼 것, D는 지문 어휘(humble, wanted)를 빌려 정정 어구와 맞지 않게 일반화한 것이다.

seed.conflict: over a shared chore that has become a ritual
seed.topicSeed: a tailor's back room in Hanoi; a pair of rival bakers over a shared chore that has become a ritual

g.passage: Two bakers share my scale. Every morning before I open, Wira and Arisa come through the back door of the shop with their sacks, and each accuses the other of resting a thumb on the brass pan. I have watched this for six years from behind a bolt of silk. They weigh, they quarrel about the weight, they leave by separate doors. On the wall above the scale someone keeps a chalk tally in two columns, and I have never asked whose hand it is. Last winter Arisa went to her sister's in Hai Phong for a month. Wira came at the usual hour, weighed his flour, and then, without a word to me, weighed out a second sack and set it by the door Arisa always used. He frowned at the pan for a long while, lifted his thumb from the edge, and weighed it again. Each morning the second column on the wall grew by one mark.
g.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Two rival bakers share a scale and argue each morning over its fairness.
Two rival bakers keep up a morning quarrel that quietly binds them together.
One baker, left alone, keeps weighing flour at the usual hour each morning.
Two rival bakers grow closer because one baker's absence ends their quarrel.
g.explanation: 앞부분의 사건은 두 제빵사가 매일 아침 저울을 두고 서로 엄지를 올린다고 다투는 장면이다. 중간의 두 칸짜리 분필 기록은 설명 없이 남지만, 뒷부분에서 Arisa가 없는 동안 Wira가 그녀 몫까지 달고 자기 엄지를 떼어 다시 재며 두 번째 칸이 계속 늘어난다. 이 두 사건을 겹치면 다툼 자체가 둘을 묶는 의식이었음이 드러나므로 B가 정답이다. A는 사건 1만, C는 사건 2만 말하며, D는 부재가 다툼을 끝내 가까워졌다고 인과 방향을 뒤집었다.

seed.relationship: a gardener and the house's new owner
seed.openingStyle: 대명사 I 또는 We 로 시작
seed.topicSeed: a train-station cafe in Shanghai; a gardener and the house's new owner while hiding a small failure

g.passage: I met Ayesha for the first time at the cafe in Shanghai South Station, where she thanked me for keeping her late uncle's garden exactly as he had left it. I accepted the thanks and the green tea. I did not mention the plum tree by the gate, which had died in March and which I had replaced, at my own cost, with one from a nursery in Songjiang. In my coat that day was a folded receipt that I kept meaning to throw away. A year later we met at the same table. Ayesha slid a photograph across to me: her uncle, young, beside the gate, the plum tree behind him already thick and crooked. She asked whether I thought a tree could straighten itself with age. I said some did. She nodded, put the photograph back in her bag, and ordered us both another pot.
g.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A gardener accepts praise for a garden while concealing a costly replacement.
A new owner shares an old photograph of her uncle beside the garden gate.
A gardener's hidden repair is likely seen through and tactfully left unspoken.
A gardener's silence about a repair makes the owner doubt his other work.
g.explanation: 사건 1에서 화자는 정원을 그대로 지켜 줬다는 감사를 받으면서 죽은 매화나무를 몰래 바꿔 심은 사실을 숨긴다. 1년 뒤 사건 2에서 Ayesha는 원래 나무가 굵고 굽어 있던 사진을 보여 주며 나무가 곧게 펴질 수 있는지 묻고, 화자의 얼버무림에 고개만 끄덕인 뒤 차를 더 주문한다. 두 사건을 함께 읽으면 화자의 숨김이 이미 간파되었으나 조용히 묻어 두어졌음을 알 수 있어 C가 정답이다. A는 사건 1만, B는 사건 2의 표현만 빌렸고, D는 침묵이 의심을 낳았다고 관계를 뒤집었으나 지문에는 그런 의심의 행동이 없다.

seed.relationship: a ranger and a lost hiker
seed.conflict: over an apology offered too late
seed.topicSeed: a soccer field at dusk in Jeju Island; a ranger and a lost hiker over an apology offered too late

g.passage: By the autumn of 1931 the ranger Eunseo had given up the mountain and taken the job of marking the school field in lime. Eleven years earlier she had found a hiker named Bokhee in the fog below the crater, half a day off the trail, and had walked him down without once letting go of his collar, saying in front of the whole village that a fool deserved the fog. He had left the island the next week. She still kept, in her coat, the collar button that had come off in her hand. At dusk one evening a man came onto the field with a dozen boys and a ball. He set them in a row along her fresh white line and told them that anyone who crossed it before the whistle would run the field twice. Eunseo started toward him, the words she had saved ready in her mouth. Bokhee raised his hand to her, then blew his own whistle, and the boys ran.
g.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A ranger once shamed a lost hiker publicly while leading him to safety.
A man trains a row of boys to wait for his whistle at a line.
A ranger's later regret leads her to treat a returning hiker more gently.
A ranger's old harshness lives on in the hiker's teaching, overtaking her apology.
g.explanation: 앞부분의 사건 1에서 Eunseo는 길 잃은 Bokhee를 멱살 잡듯 끌고 내려오며 마을 사람들 앞에서 망신을 준다. 중간의 단추는 설명 없이 남지만, 뒷부분 사건 2에서 Bokhee는 아이들을 그녀가 그은 선에 세우고 휘파람 전에 넘지 말라고 엄하게 가르친다. Eunseo가 준비한 말을 꺼내기도 전에 그는 손을 들고 휘파람을 불어, 그녀의 엄격함이 이미 그의 가르침이 되어 사과를 앞질렀음이 드러나므로 D가 정답이다. A는 사건 1만, B는 사건 2만 말하며, C는 그녀의 후회가 행동을 바꿨다고 인과를 뒤집었는데 지문은 그녀가 실제로 대하는 방식을 보여 주지 않는다.

seed.relationship: a daughter and her absent father's friend

seed.topicSeed: a community garden in Haifa; a daughter and her absent father's friend after discovering a letter meant for someone else

g.passage: When the garden gate opened on Thursdays, Avraham was always already inside, sorting the post that came for the plot holders into the tin box by the tool shed. He had done this since Miriam's father left for Beirut, and no one had asked him to. That morning Miriam held out an envelope she had found under the seed packets in her father's drawer, addressed in his hand to a woman in Jaffa. Avraham glanced at the postmark space, which was blank, and at the date in the corner, which was the week before her father went away. He said that the post office was on his way home and he might as well take it. He had already been through that drawer twice that spring, looking, he said, for bean seed. He slid the envelope into his inner coat pocket, not the satchel, and knelt to turn the soil in her father's empty bed.
g.question: Based on the text, why does Avraham most likely take the envelope from Miriam?
options: To post it on his way home as a small favor to Miriam
To secure a letter he had been hunting for on his own
To continue the post duties he took on for the garden's members
To spare himself questions from Miriam about her father's leaving
g.explanation: Avraham은 우체국이 집에 가는 길이라며 편지를 가져가겠다고 하지만, 이는 표면 명분이다. 앞부분에서 그는 Miriam의 아버지가 떠난 뒤 아무도 부탁하지 않은 우편 정리를 맡아 왔고, 중간에서는 이미 봄에 그 서랍을 두 번이나 뒤졌다는 사실이 드러난다. 끝에서 그는 편지를 우편 가방이 아닌 안주머니에 넣어, 부치려는 것이 아니라 스스로 찾던 편지를 확보하려 했음을 암시하므로 B가 정답이다. A는 표면 명분만, C는 습관 단서만 설명하고, D는 다른 감정을 끌어와 서랍을 미리 뒤진 순서를 설명하지 못한다.

seed.relationship: a grandson and the grandfather's old friend
seed.topicSeed: a fishing harbor in Istanbul; a grandson and the grandfather's old friend about starting over somewhere unfamiliar

g.passage: Armand had watched Fatma row his grandfather out past the breakwater every dawn of his childhood, and every dawn she had made the old man retie the bow line before she would push off. Now she was at the quay before the lamps were out, insisting on rowing him to the Marseille steamer herself. The harbor boatmen, she said, charged a boy with a trunk double. The steamer did not sail until noon. Armand had said so twice. She rowed slowly, stopping twice in the middle of the Golden Horn to make him check the ropes on his trunk, which he had tied and she had already checked on the quay. Fifty yards from the steamer's ladder she shipped her oars, folded her hands in her lap, and waited.
g.question: Based on the text, why does Fatma most likely insist on rowing Armand to the steamer herself?
options: To save him the high fare the harbor boatmen would charge
To keep up the dawn routine she once shared with his grandfather
To give him one last lesson in managing without her help
To delay a parting she was reluctant to face just yet
g.explanation: Fatma는 뱃사공들이 짐 든 소년에게 두 배를 받는다는 표면 명분을 댄다. 앞부분에서 그녀는 할아버지에게 매번 밧줄을 다시 묶게 했고, 중간에서는 정오 출항인데도 새벽에 나와 이미 확인한 밧줄을 Armand에게 두 번이나 다시 점검시킨다. 끝에서 그녀가 노를 거두고 손을 모은 채 기다리는 것은 마지막 구간을 그가 스스로 저어 가게 하려는 것이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 표면 명분만, B는 습관 단서만 설명하며, D는 이별을 미루려는 감정으로 보았으나 배 앞에서 노를 놓고 기다리는 순서를 설명하지 못한다.

seed.relationship: a landlord's son and a tenant's daughter
seed.topicSeed: a stone bridge in Marseille; a landlord's son and a tenant's daughter over an old photograph

g.passage: Whenever Mathis came for the rent, he stopped on the stone bridge below our building and asked to see my mother's photograph again, the one from 1952 with every shutter on the rue open and painted. He said his father wanted the old colors for the repairs. Theo, he called me, as if we were still twelve. In the second week of August he asked to borrow it outright. That was the week the notice went up in the lobby that the building had been sold, and the week, as everyone in Marseille knows, when no office in the city answers its telephone. He gave me a receipt in his own handwriting. A month later he brought the photograph back in a stiff envelope stamped by the city archive, with the date of a hearing penciled on the flap.
g.question: Based on the text, why does Mathis most likely borrow the photograph?
options: To match the original shutter colors for his father's repairs
To keep a reminder of the childhood he shared with Theo
To make amends to Theo's family for his father's sale
To submit it as a record for keeping the building unchanged
g.explanation: Mathis는 아버지가 수리를 위해 옛 색을 원한다는 표면 명분을 댄다. 앞부분에서 그는 월세를 걷으러 올 때마다 다리 위에서 사진을 다시 보자고 했고, 중간에서는 건물이 팔렸다는 공고가 붙은 바로 그 주에 사진을 아예 빌려 가며 아버지가 아닌 자기 손으로 영수증을 써 준다. 끝에서 사진은 시 기록 보관소 도장과 청문회 날짜가 적힌 봉투에 담겨 돌아오므로, 건물을 지키기 위한 자료로 쓰려 했다는 D가 정답이다. A는 표면 명분만, B는 습관 단서만 설명하고, C는 미안함이라는 다른 감정으로 보아 보관소·청문회로 이어지는 순서를 설명하지 못한다.

seed.conflict: about whether a small kindness was a cover for something else
seed.topicSeed: a salt flat in Chiang Mai; two estranged sisters about whether a small kindness was a cover for something else

g.passage: Chiang Mai has no sea, so the salt flat my sister Thuy rented that dry season was a shallow pan of brine a farmer had given up on, two hours east of the city. I arrived on the noon bus. She had swept a path to the hut. She had set out one cup, then a second cup. She had bought the good fish sauce, the kind our father kept on the high shelf, and left the bottle unopened beside my plate. We talked about the price of rakes. We talked about the bus. When I asked why she had written after eleven years, she said the crust needed raking before the wind came up, and went out to rake it. I stood at the door with the bottle in my hand for a long time, and then I carried a second rake out to the far end of the pan and began where she had not.
g.question: Which choice best describes the tone of the text?
options: Matter-of-fact and guardedly tender toward a returning sister
Dry and amused toward a sister's small domestic fussing
Calm and wary toward a sister's possibly hidden motives
Reserved and tender toward family and the past
g.explanation: 앞부분은 소금밭의 내력, 버스, 컵, 갈퀴 값처럼 건조한 사실을 짧은 문장으로 늘어놓아 담담한 겉 어조를 만든다. 중간의 두 번째 컵과 아버지가 아끼던 소스는 언니의 조용한 준비를 보여 주고, 끝에서 화자는 병을 든 채 오래 서 있다가 두 번째 갈퀴를 들고 나가 언니가 손대지 않은 곳부터 일을 시작한다. 이 겉 층과 속 층을 겹치면 조심스럽지만 다정한 어조인 A가 정답이다. B는 겉 층만 읽은 것이고, C는 속 층의 원인을 의심으로 뒤집었으며, D는 같은 감정군이지만 대상을 가족과 과거 전체로 넓혔다.

seed.relationship: a teacher and a student who will not speak

seed.topicSeed: a salt-water pool in Accra; a teacher and a student who will not speak over a plan that depends on a lie

g.passage: "He is my nephew, and he swims well," I told the attendant at the sea-pool, and signed the ledger in my best schoolroom hand. Babatunde stood behind me with his towel folded into a square. He had not spoken a word in my classroom since Michaelmas, and he did not speak now. The attendant took my shilling. The pool was cut into the rocks below the fort, and the tide refreshed it twice a day, and the water was green and very still. I had prepared a little speech about courage. I did not give it. When he reached the edge he stopped, and I stopped beside him, and I watched a crab work along the wall rather than his face. He went in at last without a sound. I sat on the warm rock with my boots still laced and my hand on his towel until his head came up the third time.
g.question: Which choice best describes the tone of the text?
options: Brisk and businesslike toward a pupil's seaside outing
Composed and anxiously watchful toward a wordless pupil

Calm and protective toward the children in her care
g.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 거짓말을 하고 장부에 서명하고 돈을 내는 일을 사무적으로 짧게 서술해 침착한 겉 어조를 만든다. 중간에서 준비한 연설을 하지 않고 소년의 얼굴 대신 게를 바라보는 멈칫함이 나타나고, 끝에서는 장화도 벗지 않은 채 수건에 손을 얹고 그의 머리가 세 번째로 떠오를 때까지 기다린다. 이 두 층을 겹치면 침착하지만 불안하게 지켜보는 어조인 B가 정답이다. A는 겉 층만, C는 속 층의 원인을 거짓말에 대한 불편함으로 바꾼 것이며, D는 대상을 맡은 아이들 전체로 넓혔다.
